name: Onondaga
catalog_quote: Main stress is normally penultimate, but can be final or antepenultimate under special circumstances. It can be analyzed with a syllabic trochee, with stressed suffixes and extrametrical suffixes.
sweep_summary: Both sweep items are the same work: Michelson's 1983 Harvard PhD (Glottolog 160828 hh and 136545 mpieva; the mpieva 'Cambridge' school is an error), published in revised form as Michelson 1988, A Comparative Study of Lake-Iroquoian Accent (Kluwer), the dedicated first-hand accent study behind Hayes 1995:266. No open full-text copy exists (ProQuest/UMI; Springer paywalled with JS challenge; archive.org lending-only, djvu/search-inside refused; HathiTrust search-only; Google Books API quota exhausted), but the Google Books legacy feed and the OpenLibrary search-inside API returned overlapping verbatim snippets that reconstruct the opening of section 3.4 'Onondaga Accent' (pp. 90-91): utterance-final words have penultimate stress by default (joiner included); a few final morphemes attract final stress, a few repel stress to the antepenult; utterance-medially stress is generally word-final; and (p. 91) highest pitch can separate from strongest stress. The 1983 dissertation snippets say the same ('a rule of penultimate stress identical to the Mohawk Stress Rule and Oneida Stress Rule'; utterance-medial final stress). This confirms penultimate as the position but contradicts the catalog's kind=fixed-strict: recommend recoding to fixed-penultimate dominant (non-strict) with the morphological and utterance-medial exceptions, citing Michelson 1988:90-91 in place of the Abrams 2006 footnote / Hayes summary. Full pp. 90-97 (morpheme lists, fn. 40) and Woodbury 2018 ch. 2 remain high-priority acquisitions. Everything fetched sources is with a line.

new_statements.quote: The majority of words in utterance-final position have penultimate stress. In Onondaga this is true also of words with a penultimate joiner; recall that the joiner could not be accented in PLI (cf. section 3.1.). Final stress occurs when the final morpheme in the word is one of a few morphemes that attract stress in this position; similarly, antepenultimate stress occurs when the final morpheme in the word is one of a few morphemes that repel stress. In utterance-medial position, stress is generally word-final, but a few suffixes that cannot be stressed condition penultimate stress.
new_statements.citation: Michelson, Karin. 1988. A Comparative Study of Lake-Iroquoian Accent (Studies in Natural Language and Linguistic Theory 12). Dordrecht: Kluwer. Section 3.4 'Onondaga Accent', pp. 90-91 (published revision of the 1983 Harvard dissertation that is the sweep's target item).
new_statements.locator: sect. 3.4, pp. 90-91 (opening paragraph of the Onondaga section; 3.4.1 'Separation of Pitch and Stress' begins p. 91); DOI of the chapter 10.1007/978-94-009-2709-4_3
new_statements.reading: Penultimate stress is the default for utterance-final (citation-form) words, joiner vowels counting as syllables; a small closed set of final morphemes attracts final stress and another small set repels stress onto the antepenult; utterance-medially stress is generally word-final. So Onondaga is fixed-penultimate as the dominant pattern with morphologically conditioned final/antepenultimate exceptions and a phrase-position alternation, not exceptionless penultimate: keep position=penultimate, drop strict=true (move to the dominant set), and note the utterance-medial final-stress rule and the pitch/stress separation (p. 91). Caveat: text recovered from overlapping verbatim snippets (Google Books feed + OpenLibrary search-inside of the archive.org scanned), not from an open full-text copy; the stitched passage is consistent across both sources and with the held Hayes 1995:266 summary and the on-disk Julian 2010 pins to Michelson 1988:90-97.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both Abrams 2006 quotations are verbatim at the stated places in the held text (p. 12 fn. 7; pp. 19-20), and the Hayes 1995:266 Onondaga paragraph is held and reads as the record says. sources.quote: I assume that Onondaga has a rule of penultimate stress that is identical to the Mohawk Stress Rule and Oneida Stress Rule. Under certain conditions high pitch (and perhaps also strong stress) occurs on the antepenult or even on ... Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca also distinguish utterance-medial from utterance-final position, but in these languages the distinction is restricted to stress. In utterance-medial position certain forms have final stress whereas the corresponding utterance-final forms have penultimate or prepenultimate stress.
sources.locator: Onondaga accent section (chapter on Onondaga; Google Books feed exposes no page numbers); the seven-syllable example is numbered (37)
sources.note: Onondaga has a penultimate stress rule identical to Mohawk/Oneida; under certain conditions high pitch (and perhaps stress) lands on the antepenult or earlier (epenthetic vowels are counted for stress but ignored for highest pitch, quoting Chafe 1977:174); utterance-medial forms can have final stress where the utterance-final form has penultimate or prepenultimate stress. Confirms the penultimate default; contradicts a 'strict' coding (final and antepenultimate stress exist; utterance-medial final stress).
